newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries off at midday, 10-yr sales cancelled.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries off at midday, 10-yr sales cancelled.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were off session lows at midday on Monday after the U.S. Treasury said it would not hold 10-year note auctions originally scheduled for July and October.

"The downward bias is just some consolidation following Friday's awfully large run-up on buying that was largely technical in nature," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds. "What's helping to limit some losses is the Treasury's cancellation of its off-cycle 10-year note auctions."
At noon EDT/1600 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was priced at 97-24/32 down 9/32 from Friday's close to yield 6.80 percent.

The 30-year bond yield ended at 6.78 percent on Friday, its lowest closing yield since February 28, after buying by foreign investors, domestic retail accounts, technical factors and short-covering spurred the market higher, erasing losses incurred after the release of the May U.S. employment report.
Flanagan said the "problems the dollar is having on world foreign exchange markets" also weighed on Treasury prices.
The dollar was lower against the mark at midday as the German unit strengthened on the possibility of an EMU delay.

What trimmed the sharpest of the morning's losses was the U.S. Treasury's announcement that it would scrap its sales of conventional 10-year notes in July and October. It introduced a new five-year inflation-protected security.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said at a news conference that a lower federal budget deficit and the success of the inflation-indexed securities that the Treasury began to sell last January had allowed the Treasury to eliminate two of six annual sales of fixed-rate 10-year notes.
